title: Tzav: seven days at the door (Leviticus 8:33–35)
hookLine: the priests wait seven days at the entrance before serving

cards: The robes are on. The oil has been poured on Aaron's head. The blood is on ear, thumb and toe.

Everything is ready. In a movie, the next scene would be Aaron striding into the sanctuary to begin his life's work. Instead, Moses gives the new priests an instruction that sounds almost like a letdown.
Don't go anywhere. Stay right here, at the entrance of the tent, day and night. Not for an hour.
For a week. The work they've been dressed for will have to wait.

teach.b: The verses say: you shall not go out from the entrance of the tent of meeting for seven days, until the days of your ordination are complete. Stay at the entrance day and night, and keep the charge of the Lord.
The Hebrew for these days of ordination is milu'im, from a root meaning filling. In biblical Hebrew, to ordain a priest is literally to fill his hands.
So these are filling days: not days of doing, but days of being filled.
What were they doing at the door all week? The text doesn't say much. The offerings were repeated each day, and the priests ate their portion at the entrance.
Mostly, they waited, in the doorway between the camp and the holy place, neither outside nor fully in. And seven isn't a random number. It's the length of creation, the week every Jew lives by.
The rabbis took this week seriously enough to build on it.
The Talmud, at the start of the tractate on Yom Kippur, learns from these verses that the high priest should be set apart for seven days before the holiest day of the year, to prepare.

The Mishnah sets apart the priest who burned the red heifer for seven days as well. Here, the holiest work doesn't start the moment someone is ready. It starts after a week in the doorway, hands being filled.

how: Following the Talmud's reading of these verses, the high priest in the Second Temple was set apart for seven days before Yom Kippur to prepare for the day's service.

games.q: you're Aaron. you're anointed, dressed and marked, ready to serve. what does Moses tell you to do?
o: stay at the entrance of the tent for seven days.
games.why: stay at the entrance day and night for seven days, until the days of ordination are complete. the work waits.

practice: Think of something big you're about to start, or want to: a move, a project, a hard conversation, a new habit. Instead of planning it, stand at its entrance for a minute, and notice what you hope for and what you're afraid of.
Rest your hands open in your lap, empty, the way the priests' hands were before they were filled.
